nameStory: The dwarf waterlily gets its name from being much smaller than its common cousin, the American white waterlily. It's also called Leiberg's waterlily after John Bernhard Leiberg, a Swedish-American botanist who explored and cataloged plants across the northern United States in the late 1800s. This tiny treasure was named in his honor for his contributions to understanding our northern flora.
description: The dwarf waterlily is like finding a miniature version of the classic pond waterlily we all know and love. This petite aquatic plant floats its small, rounded leaves and delicate white flowers on the surface of northern ponds and slow streams. Everything about this plant is scaled down - smaller leaves, smaller flowers, and overall more compact than its larger relatives. It's an emergent aquatic plant, meaning it's rooted underwater but sends its leaves and flowers up to float on the surface.

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Noticeably smaller in all parts compared to common waterlilies - leaves, flowers, and overall scale are distinctly miniature, giving it a delicate, almost toy-like appearance

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small, rounded floating leaves with a slit from edge to center where the stem attaches, deep green and waxy to the touch with a smooth, almost rubbery texture

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white flowers with multiple petals that feel papery when touched, floating on the water surface and often appearing almost too small to be a 'real' waterlily

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms small colonies in shallow areas of ponds and slow streams, with leaves and flowers scattered across the water surface rather than densely packed

habitat: Look for dwarf waterlily in quiet, shallow ponds and slow-moving streams across northern New England, particularly in areas with soft, muddy bottoms. It prefers cooler waters and is often found in the same types of habitats as other northern specialties. This is an extremely rare find in our region - so rare that it's been documented only once in New England according to current records.

seasonality.spring: New leaves begin emerging and unfurling on the water surface as waters warm, appearing as small green discs floating up from below.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season when the delicate white flowers appear, floating alongside the mature leaves on the water surface.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and leaves begin to yellow and sink as the plant prepares for winter dormancy.
seasonality.winter: Completely dormant with all above-water parts gone, surviving as roots and underground stems in the pond bottom.

funFact: This tiny waterlily is so rare in New England that it's been spotted only once in the entire region - making it potentially rarer here than finding a four-leaf clover, which statistically appears in about 1 in 5,000 to 10,000 three-leaf clovers!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with young American white waterlilies, but dwarf waterlily remains small even when mature - if you find waterlily leaves and flowers that seem unusually tiny and delicate, and stay that way throughout the season, you might have found this rare gem.
contextualKnowledge: The dwarf waterlily is listed as state threatened in Maine, Michigan, and Minnesota, highlighting just how uncommon this species is throughout its range. In New England, finding one would be an exceptional botanical discovery worthy of reporting to local naturalist groups.
compareHints: Compared to the American white waterlily, its only close relative in New England, dwarf waterlily is dramatically smaller in every dimension and tends to grow in cooler, more northern waters. While American white waterlily can have leaves 6-12 inches across, dwarf waterlily's leaves rarely exceed a few inches, and the flowers are proportionally much smaller and more delicate.

relatedSpecies.distinction: American white waterlily is much larger and more robust than its only regional relative, the dwarf waterlily, which has leaves under 4 inches across and grows in more northern, acidic bog waters.
